blocks.content: You pay for something with Stripe and, seconds later, the merchant emails you a receipt and ships your order. You push code to GitHub and a build kicks off on its own. Someone sends a text to your app number and Twilio delivers it to your server instantly.

In none of these cases is your server sitting there asking, again and again, has anything happened yet. Instead, the other service reaches out to you the moment the event occurs. That reach out is a webhook.
A webhook flips the usual direction of an API. Normally your server calls someone else. With a webhook, someone else calls your server. It is often described as a reverse API, or an HTTP callback.
Once you learn to spot them, you see webhooks behind most integrations you use: payment receipts, chat bots, CI pipelines, shipping updates, and the automation tools that wire apps together.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278439441-897302359.png
blocks.alt: A webhook: the provider calls you the instant something happens

blocks.content: 1. What a Webhook Is

A webhook is an HTTP request that one service sends to another to announce that an event has happened. When you register a webhook, you give a provider a URL, and the provider promises to send an HTTP POST to that URL whenever a chosen event occurs.

The request body carries the details of the event, usually as JSON. Your server reads it, does whatever it needs to do, and replies with a success status so the provider knows the message was received.

The important mental shift is direction. With a normal API call, you are the client and you make the request when you want data. With a webhook, you are the server, and the provider makes the request to you when it has news. You are no longer pulling, you are being pushed to.

["Event driven: it fires only when something actually happens","Server to server: one backend calling another backend over HTTP","Push based: the provider initiates, you receive","Just HTTP: a plain POST to a URL you control, usually with a JSON body"]
items: Event driven: it fires only when something actually happens
Server to server: one backend calling another backend over HTTP
Push based: the provider initiates, you receive
Just HTTP: a plain POST to a URL you control, usually with a JSON body

blocks.content: People call it a reverse API because the roles are swapped. Your public endpoint behaves like an API that the provider consumes, rather than the other way around.

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: A webhook is a POST request a provider sends to your URL the moment an event happens, so you learn about it instantly instead of polling for it.

An everyday analogy: polling is calling the shop every ten minutes to ask if your order is ready. A webhook is leaving your phone number so the shop calls you the moment it is done. Far less effort, and you hear about it the instant it happens.
The name callback captures this well. You hand the provider a way to call you back, and it does so when there is something to report.
So there are always two roles: the provider that sends, and the consumer that receives. Most of the time you are the consumer, wiring your app to react to a service like Stripe or GitHub.
2. Why Webhooks Exist
To see why webhooks matter, imagine you had to build a payment flow without them.

Your only option would be polling. Every few seconds you would call the payment provider and ask, is order 123 paid yet. Most of those calls would come back with no change. You would be making thousands of pointless requests, hammering their API, and still learning about each payment several seconds late.

Now flip it. Instead of you asking constantly, the provider simply tells you the instant the payment succeeds. One request, sent exactly when it matters, carrying exactly the data you need. That is the entire value of a webhook.

["No wasted requests: nothing is sent until an event actually happens","Near instant: you learn about the event the moment it occurs, not on the next poll","Less load on both sides: no constant polling traffic to absorb","Simpler logic: you react to events instead of managing a polling loop and tracking what you have already seen"]
items: No wasted requests: nothing is sent until an event actually happens
Near instant: you learn about the event the moment it occurs, not on the next poll
Less load on both sides: no constant polling traffic to absorb
Simpler logic: you react to events instead of managing a polling loop and tracking what you have already seen

blocks.content: The numbers make it stark. Suppose ten thousand merchants each poll for payment updates every five seconds. That is two thousand requests per second of mostly empty polling, all day, for events that happen only occasionally. Webhooks replace that whole flood with one request per real event.
That efficiency is not only about cost. Less traffic means fewer rate limit problems, simpler code, and lower latency, all at once.

Polling also has an awkward tradeoff you escape entirely. Poll too often and you waste resources and hit rate limits, poll too rarely and you are slow. A webhook has no interval to tune, it just fires when needed.

This is why almost every serious platform, from payments to source control to messaging, offers webhooks. They are the standard way for one backend to notify another that something happened, without the receiver having to ask over and over.

blocks.title: Webhooks are for server to server
blocks.content: Webhooks notify your backend, not a user browser. To push updates all the way to a user screen, you still use SSE or WebSockets. Webhooks and those techniques often work together.
3. How Webhooks Work
The lifecycle of a webhook is short and clear once you see it laid out.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278441461-47540158.png
blocks.alt: The provider posts to your endpoint when an event happens, you reply 200

blocks.content: ["You expose a public URL, for example an endpoint like /webhooks/stripe","You register that URL with the provider and choose which events you care about","An event happens on the provider side, such as a payment or a new commit","The provider sends an HTTP POST to your URL with the event details in the body","Your server reads the event, does its work, and replies with a 2xx status","The provider sees the success and considers the event delivered"]
items: You expose a public URL, for example an endpoint like /webhooks/stripe
You register that URL with the provider and choose which events you care about
An event happens on the provider side, such as a payment or a new commit
The provider sends an HTTP POST to your URL with the event details in the body
Your server reads the event, does its work, and replies with a 2xx status
The provider sees the success and considers the event delivered

blocks.content: That success reply is more important than it looks. The provider is watching for it. If your server does not answer, or answers with an error, the provider assumes delivery failed and will try again later. We will come back to those retries, because they shape how you must build the receiver.

One requirement follows immediately: your endpoint has to be reachable from the public internet. During development it is running on your laptop, which is not, so you need a tunnel to expose it, which we cover in the testing section.

It is worth internalising that you do not control when a webhook arrives. It comes when the event happens, which could be at 3am, during a deploy, or in a burst of hundreds at once. Your endpoint has to be ready at all times, not just when you are watching.
The payload itself is just JSON you agree on with the provider. A typical event has a type, a unique id, a timestamp, and a data object with the details, plus a signature header for verification.
This always on nature is exactly why webhooks pair so well with a queue. A sudden burst is absorbed instead of dropped, which we look at shortly.
4. A Real Example: A Stripe Payment
blocks.text: 4. A Real Example: A Stripe Payment

blocks.content: Payments are the classic webhook use case, so let us trace one end to end with Stripe.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278443154-131580923.png
blocks.alt: A customer pays, Stripe posts a signed event, you verify and fulfil the order

blocks.content: A customer clicks pay. The card is charged by Stripe, not by your server, so at that moment your backend does not yet know the payment succeeded. This is the key insight: the important event happened on someone else system.

The instant the charge succeeds, Stripe sends a POST to your webhook URL with an event object, something like payment_intent.succeeded, containing the amount, the customer, and your order reference. It also includes a signature header that proves the request really came from Stripe.

Your server verifies that signature, replies 200 to acknowledge it, and then does the real work: marking the order as paid, sending a receipt, and starting fulfilment. From the customer point of view, the receipt arrives seconds after paying, with no page refresh and no polling.

blocks.title: Why not just trust the browser
blocks.content: You might think the browser could tell your server the payment worked. It cannot be trusted, because a user could fake that call or simply close the tab. The webhook comes straight from Stripe, server to server, so it is the source of truth.

There is a failure case to plan for. What if the webhook never arrives, because your server was down for the whole retry window? For money you never want to silently miss a payment. The safety net is reconciliation: periodically pull recent state from the provider and compare, so anything a webhook missed is caught.

blocks.title: Webhooks plus reconciliation
blocks.content: Use webhooks for speed and a periodic reconcile job for safety. Webhooks handle the normal case instantly, and reconciliation guarantees nothing is permanently lost if a delivery fails.
In practice teams reconcile once a day for low value events, and more often or on demand for money. The right cadence depends on how costly a missed event would be.
5. Building an Endpoint to Receive Webhooks
blocks.text: 5. Building an Endpoint to Receive Webhooks

blocks.content: Receiving a webhook is just handling a POST request, but there are a few details that matter a lot.

Notice the raw body. Signature verification hashes the exact bytes the provider sent, so if a framework parses the JSON first, the bytes change and the signature no longer matches. You must capture the raw body on webhook routes.

Notice also how little happens inside the handler. It verifies, enqueues, and replies. The heavy work of fulfilling the order runs later in a worker. This keeps the response fast, which matters because providers expect a quick acknowledgement.

Finally, the endpoint returns a clear status. A 2xx means delivered, and anything else signals failure and triggers a retry. Being deliberate about the status code you return is part of building a correct receiver.
A real handler also routes by event type, because you subscribe to several and they all arrive at the same URL.

The default case simply ignores unknown types and still returns 200. Providers add new event types over time, and you do not want an unrecognised event to look like a failure and trigger endless retries.
Keep the handler small and boring. The less it does before returning 200, the fewer ways it can fail or time out under load.
6. Securing Webhooks with Signatures

Here is the uncomfortable truth about a webhook endpoint: it is a public URL that accepts POST requests. Anyone who finds it can send it fake events. If you trusted every request, an attacker could POST a fake payment succeeded and get free products.

The defense is a signature. The provider and you share a secret. When the provider sends an event, it computes a hash of the payload using that secret and puts the result in a header, for example Stripe-Signature or GitHub X-Hub-Signature. Your server recomputes the same hash and checks that they match.
Because only you and the provider know the secret, no attacker can forge a valid signature. A request without a correct signature is rejected immediately.

["Always verify the signature before trusting or acting on an event","Compare hashes with a timing safe comparison, not a normal equals, to avoid leaking information through timing","Use the raw request body for the hash, exactly as received","Keep the signing secret in configuration, never in code or the client"]
items: Always verify the signature before trusting or acting on an event
Compare hashes with a timing safe comparison, not a normal equals, to avoid leaking information through timing
Use the raw request body for the hash, exactly as received
Keep the signing secret in configuration, never in code or the client

blocks.content: The exact header differs by provider. Stripe uses Stripe-Signature, GitHub uses X-Hub-Signature-256, and others have their own, but the idea is always the same: a keyed hash of the payload that only the holder of the secret could produce.
Rotate the signing secret if it ever leaks, and support two valid secrets briefly during a rotation so you do not drop events while switching.
Verifying is cheap and the provider libraries do the hashing for you, so there is no excuse to skip it. One line of library code stands between you and forged events.
Many providers also include a timestamp in the signed data and reject requests that are too old. This stops a replay attack, where an attacker captures a valid request and sends it again later.

blocks.title: This is the number one webhook mistake
blocks.content: Skipping signature verification is the most common and most dangerous webhook bug. An unverified endpoint is an open door. Verify every request before you act on it.
7. Reliability: Retries, Idempotency, and Ordering
Webhooks travel over the network, and networks fail. Your server might be down, slow, or mid deploy when an event fires. Providers plan for this, and so must you.

If a provider does not receive a 2xx, it retries, usually several times with exponential backoff over minutes or hours. This is good, it means a brief outage does not lose events. But it has a direct consequence: you will sometimes receive the same event more than once.

This is called at least once delivery. The event is guaranteed to arrive at least once, but possibly twice or more. If your handler is not careful, a retried payment event could charge a customer twice or send two receipts.
The fix is idempotency. Every event has a unique id. Before processing, record that id, and if you see it again, skip the work and just reply 200.

Ordering is the other subtlety. Webhooks are not guaranteed to arrive in the order the events happened, because retries and network timing can reorder them. If order matters, do not rely on arrival order. Use timestamps or version numbers in the event, or fetch the current state from the provider when you need the truth.

blocks.title: Design for duplicates
blocks.content: Assume every webhook can arrive more than once and out of order. An idempotent handler that keys off the event id turns this from a scary problem into a non issue.

A concrete horror story shows why this matters. A payment webhook is delivered, your worker charges a wallet, but the response is slow, so the provider retries. Without idempotency the second delivery charges the wallet again. Keying on the event id makes the retry a harmless no operation.

For ordering, imagine a subscription created and then immediately cancelled. If the cancel event somehow arrives first, naive code leaves the subscription active. Using the event timestamps or a version field, rather than arrival order, avoids this.
The mental model to carry into any event system is that at least once plus idempotent equals effectively once. You cannot stop duplicates from arriving, but you can make them harmless.
8. Acknowledge Fast, Process Asynchronously

Providers expect a quick response, often within a few seconds. If your handler does slow work before replying, such as calling other services or writing lots of data, you risk timing out. The provider then thinks delivery failed and retries, even though you were busy succeeding.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785278444820-22983808.png
blocks.alt: Verify, enqueue, return 200 fast, and let a worker do the heavy processing

blocks.content: The standard pattern solves this cleanly. The webhook handler does only the fast, essential steps: verify the signature, do a quick validity check, put the event on a queue, and return 200. A separate worker then pulls from the queue and does the real processing at its own pace.

["The endpoint stays fast, so you never time out the provider","A slow downstream service no longer blocks the acknowledgement","The queue gives you retries and buffering for your own processing","A spike of events is absorbed by the queue instead of overwhelming your handler"]
items: The endpoint stays fast, so you never time out the provider
A slow downstream service no longer blocks the acknowledgement
The queue gives you retries and buffering for your own processing
A spike of events is absorbed by the queue instead of overwhelming your handler

blocks.content: The queue can be anything from a managed service like SQS to Redis or Kafka, depending on scale. The point is simply that the network facing handler and the business logic are decoupled by a durable buffer.
It also gives you a natural place to add monitoring. You can watch queue depth to see if processing is falling behind, and alert long before customers notice.
This accept fast, queue, process reliably shape is not only for external webhooks. It is a pattern you will reuse constantly for any internal event system too.
This separation also improves reliability on your side. Even if processing fails, the event is safely on the queue and can be retried without asking the provider to resend it.
The rule of a good webhook receiver: acknowledge in milliseconds, process in the background. Never make the provider wait for your slow work.
9. Webhooks vs Polling vs WebSockets and SSE
blocks.text: 9. Webhooks vs Polling vs WebSockets and SSE

blocks.content: Webhooks are one of several ways systems learn about events. Seeing them beside the others makes the fit obvious.

{"headers":["Aspect","Polling","Webhooks","WebSockets or SSE"],"rows":[["Who initiates","You ask repeatedly","The provider calls you","A persistent connection"],["Direction","You to the provider","Provider to your server","Server to a browser"],["Latency","Delayed by the interval","Near instant","Instant"],["Connection","Repeated requests","No persistent connection","One long lived connection"],["Best for","Simple, low frequency","Server to server events","Live updates in the browser"]]}
The key distinction: webhooks are server to server, provider to your backend. WebSockets and SSE push all the way to a user browser. They are not competitors, they are different legs of the journey.

In fact they combine beautifully. Stripe sends your backend a webhook when a payment succeeds, and your backend then uses SSE or WebSockets to update the user screen live. Webhook for the machine to machine hop, SSE for the last hop to the human.
And if you truly cannot miss an event, you pair the webhook with a reconcile poll, getting the speed of push and the certainty of pull together.
So a clean way to describe the landscape: polling is pull, webhooks are push between servers, and WebSockets or SSE are push to the browser.
10. Real Providers and Common Events
Webhooks are everywhere once you notice them. A quick tour of familiar ones makes the idea concrete.

["Stripe: payment_intent.succeeded, invoice.paid, charge.refunded","GitHub: push, pull_request, issues, so CI systems can react to code changes","Slack: messages and events, so bots can respond to what happens in a channel","Twilio: an incoming SMS or a call status change delivered to your server","Shopify: orders created, products updated, so your systems stay in sync"]
items: Stripe: payment_intent.succeeded, invoice.paid, charge.refunded
GitHub: push, pull_request, issues, so CI systems can react to code changes
Slack: messages and events, so bots can respond to what happens in a channel
Twilio: an incoming SMS or a call status change delivered to your server
Shopify: orders created, products updated, so your systems stay in sync

blocks.content: The pattern is identical across all of them. You register a URL, pick the events, and they POST to you with a signed payload when those events happen. Once you understand one provider, you understand them all.

One design choice varies between providers: how much data the webhook carries. A thin payload sends only an id and an event type, and expects you to call the API to fetch the full object. A fat payload includes all the details up front.

Thin payloads keep the message small and force you to read fresh data, which sidesteps ordering issues. Fat payloads save an API call but can be stale by the time you process them. Knowing which style a provider uses shapes your handler.
Zapier, IFTTT, and similar tools are essentially webhook hubs. They receive an event from one app and fire an action in another, which is why almost every product exposes them.

This is also why webhooks are the glue of modern integrations and automation tools. Services like Zapier are, at their core, huge webhook routers: they receive an event from one app and trigger an action in another.
11. Testing and Debugging Webhooks
Webhooks are awkward to develop locally, because the provider needs a public URL but your code runs on your laptop. A few tools make this painless.

["A tunnel like ngrok exposes your local server on a temporary public URL, so the provider can reach it while you debug","Provider command line tools, such as the Stripe CLI, forward real events straight to your local endpoint","Inspection sites like webhook.site give you a throwaway URL that shows exactly what a provider sends","Most dashboards log every delivery, show the payload and your response, and let you replay a past event with one click"]
items: A tunnel like ngrok exposes your local server on a temporary public URL, so the provider can reach it while you debug
Provider command line tools, such as the Stripe CLI, forward real events straight to your local endpoint
Inspection sites like webhook.site give you a throwaway URL that shows exactly what a provider sends
Most dashboards log every delivery, show the payload and your response, and let you replay a past event with one click

blocks.content: That replay button is a lifesaver. When a handler has a bug, you fix the code and replay the same event instead of trying to recreate the original payment or push by hand.

When debugging, always check three things: did the request arrive, did the signature verify, and what status did you return. The provider dashboard usually shows all three, which quickly tells you whether the problem is on their side, in your verification, or in your processing.

blocks.title: Watch the raw body in tests
blocks.content: A frequent local bug is a body parser running before your webhook route, which breaks signature checks. If verification fails only in your app but the payload looks right, suspect the raw body.

In production, log every webhook you receive with its event id, type, signature result, and the status you returned. When something goes wrong weeks later, that log is how you prove whether an event arrived and what you did with it.
Keep a separate endpoint or secret for staging, so test events from a provider sandbox never touch production data.
A good rule while integrating: build and test the receiver against replayed real events before going live, so you meet the real payload shape rather than a guess at it.
12. Delivering Webhooks at Scale
So far we have been the receiver. It is worth flipping to the provider side, because interviewers often ask how you would build a system that sends webhooks to thousands of customers.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028628-44705747.png
blocks.alt: A provider retries failed deliveries with backoff, then dead letters the rest

blocks.content: When an event happens, you do not POST to customer endpoints inline, because a slow or dead customer endpoint would block your main flow. Instead you put the event on a queue, and a fleet of delivery workers reads from it and makes the HTTP calls.

["Queue every event, then let delivery workers send them, so a slow endpoint never blocks your core system","Retry failures with exponential backoff, since many endpoints are only briefly down","Give up after enough attempts and move the event to a dead letter store, then alert or let the customer replay it","Sign every payload so customers can verify it, and include an event id so they can dedupe","Track delivery status per customer so you can show them a log and let them replay"]
items: Queue every event, then let delivery workers send them, so a slow endpoint never blocks your core system
Retry failures with exponential backoff, since many endpoints are only briefly down
Give up after enough attempts and move the event to a dead letter store, then alert or let the customer replay it
Sign every payload so customers can verify it, and include an event id so they can dedupe
Track delivery status per customer so you can show them a log and let them replay

blocks.content: The hard parts are the same ones you faced as a receiver, seen from the other direction: at least once delivery, retries, and idempotency. A good provider makes its guarantees explicit, usually at least once with signed, idempotent events.
This symmetry is a nice thing to point out in an interview. Whether you are sending or receiving, the reliable design is a queue, retries with backoff, signatures, and idempotent events keyed by id.

There is also a security concern unique to the sender. Customers give you arbitrary URLs to call, so a malicious customer could point a webhook at an internal address to probe your network, which is a server side request forgery. Validate destination URLs and block internal and private ranges.

At large scale you also fan out per subscriber. One event may need delivering to many customers who each subscribed to it, each with their own retries and delivery state, which is why the queue and worker model scales so well here.
State your delivery guarantees plainly. Most providers promise at least once delivery with signed events, and publish their retry schedule so integrators know what to expect.
13. Security and Common Mistakes
Because a webhook endpoint is public and acts on real events, security is not optional. Most of it comes down to a few disciplines.

["Verify the signature on every request before doing anything else","Use https so the payload and signature cannot be read or tampered with in transit","Check the timestamp and reject old requests to block replay attacks","Return 2xx only after you have safely accepted the event, and let retries handle real failures","Rate limit and validate, since the endpoint is exposed to the whole internet"]
items: Verify the signature on every request before doing anything else
Use https so the payload and signature cannot be read or tampered with in transit
Check the timestamp and reject old requests to block replay attacks
Return 2xx only after you have safely accepted the event, and let retries handle real failures
Rate limit and validate, since the endpoint is exposed to the whole internet

blocks.content: The most common mistakes cluster around the same misunderstandings.

["Skipping signature verification, leaving the endpoint open to forged events","Parsing the body before verifying, which breaks the signature","Doing slow work in the handler and timing out, causing needless retries","No idempotency, so duplicate deliveries double charge or double send","Assuming events arrive in order, when retries can reorder them"]
items: Skipping signature verification, leaving the endpoint open to forged events
Parsing the body before verifying, which breaks the signature
Doing slow work in the handler and timing out, causing needless retries
No idempotency, so duplicate deliveries double charge or double send
Assuming events arrive in order, when retries can reorder them

blocks.title: Two habits fix most bugs
blocks.content: Verify the signature, and make the handler idempotent by event id. Those two habits alone prevent the majority of real world webhook incidents.
One more habit: treat the webhook body as untrusted input and validate it, exactly as you would validate any request from the outside world, even after the signature checks out.
Security for webhooks really comes down to two words, verify and validate. Verify who sent it, and validate what they sent.
14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: When a design involves reacting to an external event, such as a payment, a code push, or a message, webhooks are the answer, and the interviewer wants to hear the reliability details.
Frame the direction: I explain that a webhook is a reverse API, the provider posts to my endpoint when an event happens, so I react instantly instead of polling.
Lead with security: I verify the signature on every request using the shared secret and the raw body, because the endpoint is public and could receive forged events.
Design for at least once: I make the handler idempotent by keying off the event id, since providers retry and duplicates are normal.
Acknowledge fast: I verify, enqueue, and return 200 quickly, then process in a worker, so a slow downstream never times out the provider.
Know both sides: If I am the provider sending webhooks, I use a queue with retry, backoff, dead letters, signed payloads, and per customer delivery logs.

Show the whole picture: I connect it end to end, a webhook notifies my backend, my backend updates state and then uses SSE or WebSockets to update the user live, which shows I understand where each tool fits.
